A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 31 pages of v1 and 37 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, figures, and algorithm descriptions sufficient for comparison.

before.justification: Appendix F reports original synthetic simulations of EMC and MvM, including cumulative-regret curves and fitted growth rates.

after.justification: Appendix H retains the original EMC and MvM simulations and their reported outcomes.

M1.justification: The core algorithms remain, but v2 adds MvM enumeration over candidate structures and NSP-EMC's binary search for an order-extraction tolerance. Sep-MvM replaces v1's known-order peak-identification extension with full structure recovery and an EMC fallback. Appendix I also introduces a one-to-one matching variant with offline solvers and a CombUCB1 adaptation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic single-peaked recommendation task under known and unknown structure. The non-single-peaked, separated-instance, and bipartite extensions in v2 are theoretical additions, without additional evaluated datasets or scenarios.

E2.justification: The experimental comparison still contains only EMC and MvM. CombUCB1 appears in v2's theoretical bipartite analysis, not as an added experimentally evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The simulations retain U=100, K=20, unit arm costs, B=10, the same preference generation and Bernoulli rewards, and the same structural-information controls. EMC still uses horizons from 100,000 to 1,000,000 rounds, while MvM's trajectory extends to 100,000 rounds.

E4.justification: No ablations, sensitivity studies, robustness experiments, or error analyses are added or removed. The non-single-peaked extension supplies formal guarantees, while the existing peak-tie arguments are largely consolidated into Appendix G.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 random instances with 10 independent runs per instance, displaying mean regret and standard-deviation shading. Repeated-run information and uncertainty-reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: Figure 2 and its experimental findings are retained. Both texts report an EMC slope of approximately 0.694, with 0.695 in the plot legend, and MvM slopes of 0.388–0.434. No experimental result entries are added or removed.

T1.justification: V2 adds Theorem 12's hardness result for approximation beyond 3/4 in fixed-matching optimistic evaluation, guarantees for the Section 7 extensions, and Appendix I's bipartite results. It also replaces the known-peaks lower-bound construction, dropping v1 Lemma 12's K=o(T^(1/3)) restriction, and adds feasibility reasoning to the maximal-matrix proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contribution claims retain the same offline runtime and online regret rates. The discussion adds a specific inapproximability claim for optimistic evaluation with unknown order, whereas v1 presented optimistic optimization as a possible route for future improvement.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands applicability and limitation discussions: it interprets the unknown-order regret gap as a possible computational-statistical barrier, explains degradation with distance from single-peakedness, and distinguishes the tractable unit-cost bipartite variant. The separation extension also trades v1's known order and peak-only gap for unknown structure and separation between all preference values.

D1.justification: Appendix F specifies extension parameters, including Sep-MvM's KT^(2/3) timeout and NSP-EMC's search interval [0,1] and stopping tolerance 1/T. The existing simulation libraries, hardware, computation time, and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Austrin et al. (2015) and Opatrny (1979) to support the ordering-hardness reduction. The main related-work positioning remains stable. Kveton et al. (2015), used for the bipartite extension, was already cited; its additional bibliography entry is not a new work.

P1.justification: V2 moves statistical lower bounds ahead of the algorithms, presents known-structure MvM before unknown-structure EMC, reorganizes the appendices, and consolidates peak-tie remarks into Appendix G. Several proofs are substantially rewritten or compressed, and the discussion is revised. These changes extend beyond inserting new scientific content.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 retain their visual content. V2 adds Table 1 to illustrate an existing lower-bound construction and adds Sep-MvM and NSP-EMC pseudocode blocks. The separate general-preferences UCB block becomes prose, while retained displays are relocated and the surrounding layout reflows.

improvement.justification: The new hardness and misspecification results broaden the paper, and the reorganization improves its exposition. However, Appendix B replaces v1's restricted sqrt(TK) lower-bound construction with a step-profile argument that does not justify treating directional semi-bandit feedback as ordinary K-armed feedback. Appendix I also calls its bounds matching although the displayed upper bound has an extra sqrt(B) factor, and its lower-bound proof assumes B>=U beyond the theorem's stated conditions. These substantive proof and qualification concerns prevent a confident net quality judgment.
